theme: God gives gifts to men, the psalm behind Ephesians 4
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 68:1-20. This is one of the most majestic psalms in the Psalter. Paul quotes verse 18 in Ephesians 4:8. Read it as a victory procession of God, and notice what God does for the lonely and the needy.
settingTheScene: Psalm 68 is a psalm of David, probably composed for the procession of the ark into Jerusalem. It begins with the words Moses spoke when the ark set out in the wilderness (Numbers 10:35). It recalls the exodus, Sinai, the conquest, and God’s reign from Zion. In Ephesians 4, Paul takes verse 18, about God ascending on high leading captives, and applies it to Christ’s ascension and the gifts he gives his church.
observation: “God shall arise, his enemies shall be scattered; and those who hate him shall flee before him!” (v. 1).
“But the righteous shall be glad; they shall exult before God; they shall be jubilant with joy!” (v. 3).
“Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation” (v. 5).
“God settles the solitary in a home” (v. 6).
“You ascended on high, leading a host of captives in your train” (v. 18).
“And receiving gifts among men, even among the rebellious, that the LORD God may dwell there” (v. 18).
“Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears us up; God is our salvation” (v. 19).
“Our God is a God of salvation, and to GOD, the Lord, belong deliverances from death” (v. 20).
interpretation:
The psalm starts with a battle cry: “God shall arise, his enemies shall be scattered.” As smoke is driven away, so he drives them away; as wax melts before fire, so the wicked perish before God. Meanwhile, “the righteous shall be glad; they shall exult before God; they shall be jubilant with joy.” The same God who is terrifying to his enemies is the joy of his people.

Then comes one of the most tender descriptions of God in the Bible: “Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation. God settles the solitary in a home; he leads out the prisoners to prosperity.” The mighty God who rides on the clouds is also the God of orphans and widows. His kingship is shown in his care for the vulnerable. The “solitary” are the lonely, and God places them in families. This is a theme of adoption, and the church is the household where it happens.

Verses 7 to 10 recall the exodus and Sinai, when the earth shook and the heavens poured down rain. God provided for his weary inheritance. Verses 11 to 14 refer to the conquest. Verses 15 to 17 describe Mount Zion, “the mount that God desired for his abode,” contrasted with the mountains of Bashan. And then the ascent: “The chariots of God are twice ten thousand, thousands upon thousands; the Lord is among them; Sinai is now in the sanctuary. You ascended on high, leading a host of captives in your train and receiving gifts among men, even among the rebellious, that the LORD God may dwell there.”

In the psalm, the picture is of a conquering king returning in triumph, with captives and tribute. Paul in Ephesians 4:8 quotes the verse with a small change: “he gave gifts to men.” Many interpreters explain that the conqueror receives tribute from the defeated and then distributes it to his people. Christ, having conquered sin, death, and Satan in the cross and resurrection, ascended and gave gifts to his church. The psalm foretold the ascension. Interestingly, the psalm adds that the gifts are received “even among the rebellious.” Even rebels are made into those who carry gifts, as Paul himself was a rebel turned apostle.

The psalm closes this section with a blessing: “Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears us up; God is our salvation.” Daily he carries his people. And “to GOD, the Lord, belong deliverances from death.” The final victory is his.
connection: Numbers 10:35 is the opening line of the psalm. Ephesians 4:7-16 applies verse 18. Colossians 2:15 says Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities, triumphing over them in the cross. Acts 1:9-11 and 2:33 describe the ascension and the gift of the Spirit. Psalm 146:9 and Deuteronomy 10:18 also describe God’s care for the fatherless. Hebrews 4:14 and 9:24 speak of Christ entering heaven. James 1:27 says pure religion is to care for orphans and widows. Judges 5 is another victory song.
application:
Look for a fatherless, widowed, or lonely person in your church or community. Make a place for them.

Thank Christ for the gifts he has given you. Name one and put it to use.

Pray verse 19: bless the Lord who daily bears us up.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to rise up and scatter his enemies.
Thank him for being father of the fatherless and defender of widows.
Thank him for giving gifts to his people.
